Passive Infinitives for Speculation
You use passive infinitives in writing when you want to demonstrate that something is believed or is thought to happen.  This type of writing is common in articles and texts about historical events.
Look at the following example:
Euskal Herria is believed to be home to more than 3 million Basque people.
The writer wants to communicate the fact that they suppose or speculate that the population of the area is 3 million.
Common verbs used in these types of constructions are:

believe
think
report
expect
allege
consider
know
rumor
say
Take a look at some other examples of these kinds of sentences in the text:
Euskal Herria is believed to be home to more than 3 million Basque people. It is said to translate as "land of the Basque language."
This region, is known to consist of miles of green hills and thick forests.
It is reported to be dotted with picturesque villages and cities.
While about half of the Basque people are said to still dwell in villages.
It's seen in their language, which is considered to be the tie that binds all Basques.
As an old Basque was said to proclaim ...
Gerunds After Prepositions
When you use a verb after a preposition, you must use a gerund (verb+-ing).
You cannot use an infinitive after a preposition.
Some common prepositions are:

before: Take your time before answering your questions.
for: They received extra homework for not listening in class.
after: He returned home after being in France for 3 years.
in: I'm not interested in history.
on: There's no point on talking about this anymore.
at: She is good at writing stories.

Usually, we use the preposition "to" before a verb in order to show that it is in infinitive.

For example:
I want to practice the lesson with you.

images.text:
Euskal Herria is believed to be home to more than 3 million Basque people. It is said to translate as "land of the Basque language."
The early Basques decided on settling the area thousands of years ago. Through the centuries, they got used to facing Roman, Arab, French, and, most recently, Spanish conquerors. They have always survived and kept on holding out as a separate cultural group. In 1980, they officially become the Basque Autonomous Community.

This region, is known to consist of miles of green hills and thick forests. It is reported to be dotted with picturesque villages and cities. While about half of the Basque people are said to still dwell in villages, earning their living through more traditional means such as farming and fishing, many have become more interested in doing more lucrative industrial jobs and many others have decided on joining the fast growing high-tech sector.

No matter where they live, the Basque national spirit is apparent and reflected in many aspects of society. It's seen in their language, which is considered to be the tie that binds all Basques. It's in their festivals, such as the world-famous Festival of San Fermin, known for having the running of the bulls through the streets of Pamplona.
The Basques are fiercely proud and will not stand for losing any of their national identity or ancient heritage. As an old Basque was said to proclaim, "Before God was God and boulders were boulders, the Basques were already devoted to being Basques."
